strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful question: why adversarially trained networks can retain good clean generalization while exhibiting a large robust generalization gap. Explicitly requiring both behaviors makes the objective more informative than studying robust error alone.

Combining representation complexity with feature-learning dynamics offers a useful conceptual perspective. Partial signal learning followed by memorization of sample-specific noise is an interpretable candidate mechanism.
The experiments cover synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR10, with additional measurements of local and global loss flatness. These provide qualitative evidence for the phenomenon motivating the paper.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.4 is false under its stated assumptions. Consider a distribution uniform on X=±e1 with corresponding labels, radius δ=1/4, and clean classifier f(x)=x1+8x2. This satisfies boundedness, class separation, and existence of a polynomial-size clean but nonrobust classifier. With N=D samples, both atoms have substantial empirical frequency with high probability, so vanishing robust training error forces zero robust population error; no CGRO classifier exists. Additional distributional restrictions are essential. Also, Assumption 4.2 separates opposite classes, whereas Lemma 4.5 incorrectly infers disjoint neighborhoods for every pair of training samples.

The ReLU approximation argument does not establish the representation upper bound. Appendix F claims uniform o(1) approximation of the discontinuous indicator-based classifier by continuous ReLU networks, which is generally impossible across a nonzero jump. Softening the indicators requires a separate argument controlling transition regions and preserving classification margins and robust errors; none is supplied.

Theorem 5.9 conflates different threat models. Definitions 5.4–5.6 restrict perturbations to the meaningful signal direction and leave noisy patches unchanged, while Definition 3.3 measures robust training error over the entire norm ball. Small loss against the restricted adversary does not imply small robust training error under that definition. This affects the claimed CGRO conclusion, beyond merely limiting the realism of the structured-data model.

The clean-generalization proof in Theorem E.12 uses an invalid concentration argument: a nonzero cubic polynomial of Gaussian noise is not sub-Gaussian. Its stated variance proxy also omits dependence between neurons evaluated on the same noise patch. Furthermore, constant total noise memorization does not establish the asserted constant norm of every neuron's noise component. These gaps leave the central o(1) clean test error unsupported.

The synthetic experiment does not satisfy the theorem's separation condition: it sets δ=α=10, whereas Assumption 5.7 requires δ<α. The attack can therefore erase the label-bearing signal completely, making poor robust population performance unsurprising independently of the proposed learning mechanism. The image experiments also do not isolate representation limitations from optimization failure, particularly for the constant-prediction MNIST runs. Missing PGD step sizes, iteration counts, restarts, and variability across seeds limit reproduction and confidence in the robustness measurements.

The claimed lower-bound extension beyond Li et al. (2022) needs a clearer mathematical distinction. Theorem 4.7 is existential, and Appendix F again constructs linearly separable data. Allowing a broader class of clean classifiers does not itself strengthen an existential lower bound already obtainable within the linear subclass. The synthesis may still be useful, but the stated originality is insufficiently established.

The supplementary generalization claims also lack adequate justification. Appendix G retains terms involving δ², N^(-1/2)δ^(-D/2), and δ times global flatness, without deriving Theorem B.1's advertised N^(-1/(D+2)) times flatness bound for the stated radius. Proposition B.2 concerns robust versus clean population risk, not the robust population-versus-training gap. These distinctions undermine the proposed interpretation of flatness as explaining robust overfitting.
